quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten quick checks on variable cost, contribution, investment, depreciation, return on investment and the three scenarios of the feasibility study.

questions.q: The unit contribution margin (UCM) of a metre of fabric is:
options: Selling price minus all variable costs per metre
Selling price minus fixed cost per metre
questions.explain: UCM = price − variable cost (Rs 53 − 48.78 = Rs 4.22 local). Fixed costs are deducted later at plant level, so UCM is not profit.

questions.q: Which of these is treated as a variable cost per metre in Feasibility I?
options: Sizing cost on the warp yarn
questions.explain: Sizing is charged per kg of warp, so it rises with every metre woven; salaries, depreciation and administration are monthly fixed costs in Feasibility II.

questions.q: The fabric costed in the study is:
questions.explain: The lecture takes the 20×16/128×60, 63-inch 3/1 twill whose warp and weft consumption per metre (0.613 lb and 0.338 lb) were worked out in Lecture 14.

questions.q: Commission and income tax in the cost build-up are charged as:
questions.explain: Each is 1 % of the sale price, so together they are 2 % × Rs 53 = Rs 1.06 locally and 2 % × Rs 70.32 = Rs 1.41 for export.

questions.q: The 'conservative', 'normal' and 'aggressive' scenarios of Feasibility II correspond to:
options: Low, medium and high loom speeds
Local sale only, a 50/50 mix, and export only
questions.explain: The scenarios differ in the market the cloth is sold to, which fixes the monthly contribution (2.53, 4.75 and 6.97 million); the loom count is 45 in all three.

questions.q: Yarn stock is included in the total investment but not in the base for depreciation.
questions.explain: Depreciation per month = (looms + compressor + warping and sizing + construction) ÷ life ÷ 12; yarn stock is working capital that is sold on, not an asset that wears out.

questions.q: Monthly return on investment in the study is:
questions.explain: Profit after conversion cost is divided by the Rs 223.5–210 million invested; for the normal case 0.80 ÷ 215.6 = 0.37 % a month, ×12 = 4.43 % a year.

questions.q: The 'annual return ignoring depreciation (cash)' adds depreciation back because:
options: Depreciation is not a cash outflow; it only spreads the earlier investment over the years
Depreciation is paid to the bank
questions.explain: The cash actually generated each month is profit plus depreciation; on that basis the export plant returns 28.26 % against 18.97 % after depreciation.

questions.q: The 'total conversion cost' per month in Feasibility II consists of:
options: Salaries, stores and spares, overheads, administration and depreciation
questions.explain: Conversion cost is everything the plant spends to run regardless of output — the fixed costs — totalling 4.275 million in the conservative case. Yarn and packing are already in the variable cost per metre.

questions.q: What is the lecture's final conclusion about the 45-loom plant?
options: It should not be built at all
It is viable only if it is built for the export market; local-only sale loses money
questions.explain: Local-only returns about −9 % a year, a mix about 4 %, export about 19 %; the decision is not whether to build but what market to build for.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: How price, yarn prices, consumption and fixed costs flow through to contribution, profit and return — and which way each moves.

questions.q: Warp cost per metre in the worksheet is:
options: Warp consumption (lb/m) × warp price (Rs per 10 lb) ÷ 10
questions.explain: Yarn is priced per 10 lb, so 0.613 lb × Rs 460 ÷ 10 = Rs 28.20. Multiplying by 10 would give Rs 2,820 per metre.

questions.q: Sizing cost per metre is calculated as:
options: Warp lb per metre ÷ 2.2046 × Rs per kg
Warp lb per metre × 2.2046 × Rs per kg
Weft lb per metre ÷ 2.2046 × Rs per kg
Rs per kg ÷ warp lb per metre
questions.explain: Sizing is priced per kg of warp, so the warp consumption in lb is converted to kg by dividing by 2.2046: 0.613 ÷ 2.2046 × Rs 10 = Rs 2.78. Only the warp is sized.

questions.q: Contribution per loom per day equals:
options: UCM × metres per loom per day
Selling price × metres per loom per day
UCM ÷ metres per loom per day
questions.explain: Rs 4.22 × 430 m = Rs 1,815 locally and Rs 12.19 × 430 = Rs 5,242 for export; multiplying by 45 looms and 30 days gives the plant's monthly contribution.

questions.q: If the local selling price rises by Rs 1 per metre with yarn prices unchanged, the local UCM rises by:
options: Rs 0.98, because commission and tax take 2 % of the price
Nothing, because the yarn price also rises
questions.explain: Commission + tax = 2 % of price, so Rs 0.02 of each extra rupee goes with it and Rs 0.98 reaches the contribution.

questions.q: Why is the export warp cost (Rs 34.33) higher than the local warp cost (Rs 28.20) for the same consumption?
options: The export warp yarn price is Rs 560 per 10 lb against Rs 460
Export tax is added to the yarn
questions.explain: 0.613 × 560 ÷ 10 = 34.33; the export market demands better yarn, which costs more, but the export price of Rs 70.32 more than makes up for it.

questions.q: Depreciation per month in the worksheet is:
options: (Looms + compressor + warping and sizing + construction) ÷ life in years ÷ 12
questions.explain: Only the wearing assets are depreciated: (135 + 7 + 50 + 24) ÷ 10 ÷ 12 = 1.800 million for the conservative case; yarn stock is excluded.

questions.q: If the depreciation life is changed from 10 years to 5 years, the annual return on investment will:
options: Fall, but the cash return will not change
Fall, and the cash return will fall by the same amount
questions.explain: Monthly depreciation doubles, cutting profit and the ROI; cash return adds depreciation back, so it is unaffected by the life chosen.

questions.q: Doubling the number of looms with the same contribution per loom would double the monthly contribution and also double the fixed conversion cost.
questions.explain: Contribution scales with looms, but salaries, administration and overheads do not necessarily double; that is why a larger plant usually earns a better return per rupee of investment.

questions.q: Annual return on investment ignoring depreciation (cash basis) is:
questions.explain: For the aggressive case (3.32 + 1.625) ÷ 210 × 12 = 28.26 %. Option 2 is the ordinary ROI (18.97 %); option 3 ignores the running costs altogether.

questions.q: Which change would raise the local UCM the most per metre?
options: Cutting packing from Rs 0.15 to Rs 0.10
Cutting the warp yarn price from Rs 460 to Rs 440 per 10 lb
Cutting electricity from Rs 1.55 to Rs 1.50
questions.explain: The warp price cut saves 0.613 × 20 ÷ 10 = Rs 1.23 per metre; the packing, electricity and commission changes save only Rs 0.05, Rs 0.05 and Rs 0.27. Yarn is by far the largest cost.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Costing a metre and a plant with new prices: yarn costs, sizing, commission, UCM, contribution per loom, depreciation and return.

questions.q: Warp consumption is 0.613 lb per metre and the warp yarn costs Rs 500 per 10 lb. What is the warp cost per metre?
Weft consumption is 0.338 lb per metre at Rs 480 per 10 lb. What is the weft cost per metre, to the nearest paisa?
Sizing costs Rs 12 per kg of warp and the warp consumption is 0.613 lb per metre (1 kg = 2.2046 lb). What is the sizing cost per metre, to the nearest paisa?
The selling price is Rs 65 per metre; commission is 1.5 % and income tax 1 % of the sale price. What is the commission plus tax per metre, to the nearest paisa?
At a price of Rs 65 per metre the total variable cost works out at Rs 55.40. What is the unit contribution margin?
questions.explain: UCM = 65 − 55.40 = Rs 9.60 per metre.

questions.q: With a UCM of Rs 9.60 per metre and 430 m per loom per day, what is the contribution per loom per day?
questions.explain: 9.60 × 430 = Rs 4,128 per loom per day.

questions.q: Each of 45 looms contributes Rs 4,128 per day. What is the plant's contribution in a 30-day month, in rupees?
questions.explain: 4,128 × 45 = Rs 185,760 per day; × 30 = Rs 5,572,800 ≈ Rs 5.57 million a month.

questions.q: Depreciable assets (looms, compressor, preparatory and building) total Rs 200 million and are written off over 8 years. What is the depreciation per month, in Rs million to three decimal places?
questions.explain: 200 ÷ 8 = 25 million a year; ÷ 12 = 2.083 million a month.

questions.q: A plant with a total investment of Rs 220 million makes a monthly profit of Rs 2.5 million. What is its annual return on investment, as a percentage to one decimal place?
In the study's aggressive case the monthly profit is Rs 3.32 million, depreciation Rs 1.625 million and the investment Rs 210 million. The annual cash return is nearest to:
questions.explain: (3.32 + 1.625) ÷ 210 × 12 = 28.26 %. 18.97 % is the return after depreciation and 1.58 % the monthly figure.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Decisions an investor and a mill manager take from the feasibility sheet: which market, which inputs matter, and what to check when the figures move.

questions.q: An investor says the plant 'makes 7 million a month on export, so it is a good investment'. The costing engineer should point out that:
options: 7 million is the contribution; after 3.65 million of conversion cost the profit is 3.32 million, about 19 % a year
The figure should be doubled for two shifts
questions.explain: Contribution must still pay salaries, stores, overheads, administration and depreciation; the return is judged on what is left and on the Rs 210 million invested.

questions.q: The local market will take only 50 % of production. The relevant scenario and its approximate annual return are:
questions.explain: A 50/50 mix is the normal case, with contribution 4.75 million and an annual return of 4.43 %; 28 % is the aggressive cash figure.

questions.q: Yarn prices rise 10 % while selling prices stay fixed. The local UCM of Rs 4.22 will:
options: Fall by about Rs 4.32 and become negative
Rise, because the cloth is worth more
Not change, because yarn is a fixed cost
questions.explain: Warp + weft cost is Rs 43.24 per metre; 10 % of that is Rs 4.32, more than the whole Rs 4.22 margin. The local business is extremely sensitive to yarn prices.

questions.q: The manager proposes raising loom output from 430 m to 460 m per loom per day through higher efficiency. For the export case the effect on monthly contribution is roughly:
options: An extra Rs 0.49 million a month (12.19 × 30 × 45 × 30)
A fall, because yarn use rises
questions.explain: Extra contribution = UCM × extra metres: 12.19 × 30 m × 45 looms × 30 days ≈ Rs 493,700. Yarn is used per metre and is already inside the UCM.

questions.q: The conservative scenario shows a positive cash return (0.30 %) even though its profit is negative, so the plant would at least not consume cash on local sale.
questions.explain: Profit −1.74 plus depreciation 1.80 leaves +0.055 million a month: the plant barely covers its running costs and never recovers the investment, which is why the lecture calls it a losing proposition.

questions.q: Why does the aggressive scenario carry a larger yarn stock (Rs 15 million) than the conservative one (Rs 7.5 million)?
options: Export orders need dearer yarn and larger, more reliable stocks to meet delivery dates
questions.explain: The stock is lb × Rs 50; the export case plans 300,000 lb against 150,000 lb, reflecting the need to hold yarn for firm export programmes. The loom count is the same in both.

questions.q: A bank asks for the payback period of the aggressive plant on a cash basis (investment Rs 210 million, cash generation Rs 4.945 million a month). The answer is about:
questions.explain: 210 ÷ 4.945 = 42.5 months ≈ 3.5 years. Ten years is the depreciation life, not the payback.

questions.q: The building contractor quotes Rs 30 million instead of Rs 24 million for the conservative plant. The immediate effects are:
options: Higher investment and higher monthly depreciation (by 0.05 million), lowering the return
questions.explain: Construction is both invested and depreciated: 6 ÷ 10 ÷ 12 = 0.05 million extra a month, and the denominator of the return rises to 229.5 million.

questions.q: Why does the worksheet reduce salaries, stores and overheads from the conservative to the aggressive case?
options: Each scenario carries its own, more optimistic, view of what the plant costs to run
Commission is paid by the buyer
questions.explain: The lecture says each scenario has its own view of the cost to build and to run; the aggressive case assumes tighter running costs as well as the better market.

questions.q: The plant is approved on the aggressive figures but then sells only locally. The most likely outcome is:
options: A loss of about 9 % a year and a plant that cannot repay its investment
No change, because the investment is the same
questions.explain: The market, not the machinery, decides the return; the local-only contribution of 2.53 million does not cover the 4.275 million conversion cost.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Harder feasibility reasoning: break-even contribution per loom, the export share needed to pay the bills, and the traps in reading a return.

questions.q: The conservative plant's conversion cost is Rs 4.275 million a month for 45 looms over 30 days. What contribution per loom per day is needed just to break even? Round to the nearest rupee.
questions.explain: 4,275,000 ÷ 1,350 loom-days = Rs 3,167 per loom per day, against the Rs 1,815 the local market gives.

questions.q: If a loom weaves 430 m a day and must contribute Rs 3,167 a day to break even, what UCM per metre is needed? Round to the nearest paisa.
questions.explain: 3,167 ÷ 430 = Rs 7.36 per metre — between the local Rs 4.22 and the export Rs 12.19.

questions.q: Local contribution is Rs 2.53 million a month and export Rs 6.97 million. What fraction of production must be exported for the blended contribution to equal a conversion cost of Rs 3.953 million? Give the answer as a percentage to the nearest whole number.
A student computes the local UCM as Rs 53 − (28.20 + 15.04) = Rs 9.76. The error is:
options: Forgetting sizing, packing, electricity, commission and tax (Rs 5.54 together)
questions.explain: Yarn is the largest cost but not the only variable cost; the other five lines bring the total to Rs 48.78 and the UCM down to Rs 4.22.

questions.q: The normal case's contribution input is Rs 4.75 million, the average of 2.53 and 6.97. This is a fair simplification only if:
options: Half the metres go to each market at the same loom output
questions.explain: A 50/50 blend of contributions assumes equal metres in each market; a different split (or different outputs) would need a weighted average, as in the previous question.

questions.q: In the normal case the monthly profit is Rs 0.797 million on an investment of Rs 215.625 million. What is the annual return, as a percentage to two decimal places?
questions.explain: 0.797 ÷ 215.625 = 0.3696 % a month; × 12 = 4.44 % (the sheet shows 4.43 % from unrounded figures).

questions.q: Comparing a 4.43 % return on the plant with a bank deposit paying 12 %, a rational investor would:
options: Not build on the normal assumptions; only the export case (about 19 %) beats the deposit
Conclude that returns cannot be compared
questions.explain: ROI is meant for exactly this comparison; a return below the risk-free rate does not justify the risk of a mill. The lecture's answer is to build for export.

questions.q: Because the cash return of the export plant is 28 %, the plant repays its full investment in less than four years without any depreciation charge being set aside.
questions.explain: Cash return = 1 ÷ payback: 210 ÷ 4.945 ≈ 42 months ≈ 3.5 years. The depreciation charge is only an accounting spread of that same investment.

questions.q: The export warp price falls from Rs 560 to Rs 520 per 10 lb; warp consumption is 0.613 lb per metre. By how much does the export UCM rise per metre, to the nearest paisa?
questions.explain: Saving = 0.613 × (560 − 520) ÷ 10 = Rs 2.45 per metre, lifting the export UCM from 12.19 to about 14.64.

questions.q: The aggressive plant has the lowest investment (Rs 210 million) and the highest return (18.97 %). Which statement about the cause is correct?
options: The lower investment alone explains the higher return
The return comes mainly from the contribution of 6.97 million against 2.53 million; the 13.5 million lower investment adds little
Lower depreciation is the main reason
The aggressive case has more looms
questions.explain: Putting the aggressive profit of 3.32 million over the conservative investment of 223.5 million would still give 17.8 % a year; the market, not the cheaper plant, makes the difference. All three cases have 45 looms.
